In this lesson, we will explore the motor effect, learn how to predict the direction of the force using Fleming's left-hand rule, examine the equation for the force, and understand how a DC motor works.

On one side of the conductor, the two fields are in the same direction (reinforcing each other), while on the other side, they are in opposite directions (weakening each other). The conductor is pushed from the region of stronger combined field towards the region of weaker combined field.

The Role of the Split-Ring Commutator
is the critical component that allows continuous rotation:
It is a copper ring split into two halves, insulated from each other.
Each half is connected to one end of the coil.
The carbon brushes maintain contact with the commutator as it rotates.
Every half-turn, the brush contacts switch from one half of the commutator to the other, reversing the current direction in the coil.
This ensures that the side of the coil near the north pole always carries current in the same direction, so the force on it is always in the same direction.
Without the commutator, the motor would not produce continuous rotation.
The Role of the Carbon Brushes
Maintain electrical contact between the stationary power supply and the rotating commutator.
Are made of carbon (graphite) because it is a reasonable conductor, is self-lubricating, and wears down slowly.
Press against the commutator with light spring pressure.

Explain why a split-ring commutator is needed in a DC motor.

Without a commutator, the current in each side of the coil would remain in the same direction as the coil rotates. After the coil passes the vertical position (where the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field), the direction of the force on each side would reverse. The side that was being pushed up would now be pushed down, and vice versa. This would cause the coil to decelerate, stop, and reverse, oscillating back and forth instead of rotating continuously.

The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half-turn. This means that the side of the coil near the north pole always has current flowing in the same direction, so the force on it is always in the same direction. This ensures that the turning effect is always in the same rotational direction, producing continuous rotation.

"A split-ring commutator and slip rings are the same thing."

They are different. A split-ring commutator reverses the current every half-turn (used in DC motors). Slip rings maintain continuous contact without reversing the current (used in AC generators). This distinction is critical.

Describe the construction and operation of a simple DC motor.

A rectangular coil of wire (armature) mounted on an axle between the poles of a permanent magnet. A split-ring commutator is attached to the axle, and carbon brushes connect the commutator to the external DC supply.

Current flows through the coil. By Fleming's left-hand rule, one side of the coil experiences an upward force and the other a downward force (since current flows in opposite directions on the two sides). This pair of forces creates a turning effect (torque), rotating the coil. Every half-turn, the split-ring commutator reverses the current direction in the coil. This ensures the forces always act in the same rotational direction, producing continuous rotation.
Explain why a DC motor would not rotate continuously without a commutator.

Without a commutator, after the coil passes the vertical position, the direction of the force on each side would reverse (since each side has swapped position relative to the poles). The side that was pushed up would now be pushed down, and vice versa. This would cause the coil to decelerate, stop, and reverse direction, oscillating back and forth rather than rotating continuously. The commutator reverses the current every half-turn to prevent this.

Describe how a loudspeaker produces sound.

A coil of wire (voice coil) is attached to a paper cone and placed in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet. An alternating current (the audio signal) flows through the coil. By the motor effect, the coil experiences a force that pushes it back and forth as the current alternates direction. The vibrating coil moves the cone, which pushes and pulls on the air, creating sound waves.
